newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Prodi rejects talk of govt crisis over Albania.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Prodi rejects talk of govt crisis over Albania.

text.p: Prime Minister Romano Prodi dismissed talk on Saturday that his government could fall in a rift with a key ally over his plan to send 2,000 Italian troops to Albania at the head of a multinational security force.
"Some people have been betting this government will fall...over Albania," Prodi told a business gathering in northern Italy.
"I want to say that this government has a long-term outlook. It will maintain it. The government I lead was not born for a short life," he said.

Prodi is facing the toughest political challenge of his 11 months in office over the refusal of hard left party Communist Refoundation to back the deployment of the first Italian-led multinational force in post-World War Two history.
The party is not part of the centre-left coalition government but Prodi cannot command a majority in the lower house of parliament without its support.

Its leader, Fausto Bertinotti. said on Saturday he did not want to topple Prodi over Albania but insisted his party would vote 'no' when the force deployment is put to ballots in parliament's two houses next week.
"The only room (for manoeuvre) is not to have the military mission. Frankly, it doesn't seem to me that that is the government's intention," Bertinotti told reporters.

Prodi's victory in the votes on Tuesday and Wednesday is technically not in doubt since he has the backing of the main centre-right opposition bloc. But one big party in the bloc, the hard right National Alliance, said it could change its position.
"We're certainly not prepared to lend our votes in support of a Prodi government that loses the backing of Communist Refoundation," senior party official Maurizio Gasparri said.

The U.N.-authorised force of some 6,000 men from up to eight nations is due to deploy to Albania in the week starting April 14 to assist an international relief effort to the Balkan state, rocked by weeks of armed anarchy.

Refoundation's resistance has shaken Prodi's unsteady coalition to the core, raised doubts about the reaction if the force runs into trouble and, say Italian commentators, dented Italy's international credibility.
President Oscar Luigi Scalfaro, who would have to decide whether to call an early genral election if Prodi falls, appealed on Saturday for unanimous support for the force.
"National unity in the face of a delicate mission...must not suffer distinctions between government and opposition nor lacerating and dangerous divisions," he said.
Political sources said Prodi had called a coalition summit for Monday to try to restore unity ahead of the votes in the Senate (upper house) and the Chamber of Deputies (lower house).
Coalition parties are already frustrated by Refoundation's refusal to countenance welfare spending cuts in Prodi's drive to put Italy on course to join Europe's planned single currency.
They now are talking openly of either moving to an early election or ditching Refoundation and trying to form a minority government unless Bertinotti backs down on Albania.

Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini called on Saturday for a swift showdown with Refoundation but said an early election would do more harm than good. "It would mean saying goodbye to Europe," he said in a reference to Italy's bid to be part of the monetary union.
